# Summarize Long Web Articles in Safari with Apple Intelligence

> **In short:** Apple Intelligence can summarize a 3,000-word article into a short bullet list in Safari with one tap, usually in under two minutes. You'll need a recent Apple device with the feature turned on, and it works best on readable article pages — not every site.

Long articles pile up — in your reading list, your email, your group chats. Safari, the browser built into every iPhone, iPad and Mac, can now pull out the key points of any article with one tap, using Apple Intelligence, Apple's built-in AI. This guide walks you through setting it up and using it for faster reading and research, written for anyone who has never opened Apple Intelligence before.

## Before you start
- **Device:** iPhone 15 Pro or newer, or any iPad or Mac with an Apple silicon (M1, M2, M3, M4) chip or later.
- **Software:** iOS 18.1+, iPadOS 18.1+, or macOS 15.1+ (check by opening Settings > General > Software Update).
- **Apple Intelligence on:** Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri > Turn On Apple Intelligence.
- **Apple ID:** signed in to your device (any free Apple ID works).
- **Internet:** needed for the first setup download.
- **Total time:** about 5 minutes for the first-time setup, then about 90 seconds per article once it's ready.

## Step 1 — Turn on Apple Intelligence if you haven't yet
Open the **Settings** app (the gray gears icon on your home screen). Scroll down until you see **Apple Intelligence & Siri**, and tap it. On the next screen, tap **Turn On Apple Intelligence**. The first download takes a few minutes — your device may warm up slightly while it works in the background. If you don't see the Apple Intelligence option in Settings, your device is likely not on the supported list, or your Apple ID region or device language is one Apple hasn't rolled the feature out to yet.

After it finishes, a small ✨ sparkles icon starts appearing in supported apps like Mail, Messages and Safari. That icon means Apple Intelligence is on.

💬 Example: there's nothing to type here — just wait for the download bar to finish, then leave Settings open for a moment so the setup can complete.

You'll know it worked when the Apple Intelligence option reads **"Apple Intelligence is Ready"** and the ✨ sparkles icon appears in your apps.

## Step 2 — Open Safari and load a long article
Open **Safari** (the blue compass icon) on your iPhone, iPad or Mac and navigate to any article you'd like summarized — a news piece, a long blog post, a research summary. For best results, pick an article that's mostly text with clear paragraphs. Apple's summarizer works best on readable article-style pages, not on shop pages, dashboards, or sites that block text from being selected.

💬 Example: try a 2,000-3,000 word news feature on a topic you care about, like a science explainer or a long magazine piece.

You'll know it worked when the page loads normally with the article text visible — there's nothing special to do at this stage, just open the article you want summarized.

## Step 3 — Open the page settings menu
Look at the left side of Safari's address bar — there's a small icon labeled **"Aa"** (the page settings menu). On iPhone and iPad, tap it. On Mac, click it. A panel slides up with options that usually include **Show Reader**, **Website Settings**, and — on supported devices — a **Summarize** option. If you don't see Summarize in the first menu, tap **Show Reader** first; the summarize option sometimes appears once the page is in Reader view.

💬 Example: if you're reading a news article on a major publication's website, the Aa menu usually has both Reader and Summarize options ready to go.

You'll know it worked when the page reformats into a clean Reader view — no ads, no sidebars, just text and images on a plain background.

## Step 4 — Tap Summarize and wait a moment
In the menu you just opened, look for the **Summarize** option (it usually appears with a ✨ sparkles icon next to it). Tap or click it. After a moment — typically 10 to 30 seconds — a short list of bullet points appears, usually at the top of the page or in a small popover. The bullet points capture the main ideas of the article. The original text stays below, so you can keep reading if you want more detail.

💬 Example: there's nothing to type here — the summarizer runs on the article you've already loaded in Safari, and you don't need to type anything to start it.

You'll know it worked when a small section labeled **"Summary"** appears with 3 to 5 bullet points capturing the article's main points.

## Step 5 — Read the summary and decide what to do next
Read the bullet points and decide whether the article is worth your full attention. If a specific point catches your interest, scroll down to read that section of the original article. On newer versions of iOS and macOS, you may also see a related option to ask a follow-up question about the article — for example, "What's the main argument?" — which Apple Intelligence answers using the page content.

💬 Example: if the summary mentions a statistic or quote you don't fully understand, scroll to that part of the original article to read it in context before quoting or sharing it.

You'll know it worked when you can tell in 20-30 seconds whether the article deserves a full read, a skim, or a skip — and when follow-up questions return useful, page-specific answers.

## Step 6 — Try a few different articles to learn what works
Pick a different article and load it in Safari. Try one text-heavy piece (a long news feature, a Wikipedia deep-dive) and one that's more visual (a product page, a dashboard). Tap the Aa menu and Summarize for each. You'll quickly see that some articles give clean bullet-point summaries and others don't show the option at all — that's how you learn which sites support the feature. With a little practice, summarizing becomes a habit: open any article, tap Summarize, decide whether to read.

💬 Example: try summarizing a 4,000-word magazine feature and a 600-word blog post back-to-back, and notice how the bullet count and detail differ between them.

You'll know it worked when you can comfortably triage your reading list in minutes — scanning summaries instead of reading every word — and you know which sites support the feature and which don't.

## Common mistakes
- **Looking for the Summarize button in the wrong place.** It's inside the Aa page menu (left side of the address bar) or in Reader view, not on the main Safari toolbar. Look for the page settings icon, not the share or bookmark buttons.
- **Trying it on sites that block Reader mode.** Paywalled news sites, login-required pages, or interactive web apps often don't expose Reader or Summarize. Pick a public article on a different site, or open a non-paywalled version if you can.
- **Expecting perfect summaries on dense technical articles.** Apple Intelligence usually captures the main points well, but on very dense or jargon-heavy articles it may miss nuance. Treat the summary as a triage tool, not a replacement for reading carefully when the topic matters.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** When a long article pops up in your feed and you don't have 20 minutes for it, a summary tells you in 30 seconds whether it's worth the deeper read. It's a fast way to stay informed without falling behind.
- **For your business or work:** Researchers, students, and anyone doing competitive or background research can triage reading lists in a fraction of the time — scan 10 articles' summaries in the time it would take to read two in full.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one long article you've been meaning to read but haven't yet. Summarize it in Safari, decide if it's worth your full attention, and start building the habit from there.

## Try it now
Open Safari on your iPhone, iPad or Mac, find one long article you've been putting off (a long news feature, a research piece, a Wikipedia deep-dive), tap the **Aa** menu on the left side of the address bar, choose **Show Reader** if needed, then tap **Summarize**. In under two minutes, you'll know whether the article deserves your full attention — and you'll have a new habit for the next time a long read lands in your queue.
